summary: After two iterations, the Pareto search algorithm for BLIS now achieves 100% recall and 100% precision (35/35 unique Pareto tuples found, 81/81 configs correctly identified) within a 200-evaluation budget at the primary load rate (100 req/s), up from 82.9% recall in iteration 1. The same algorithm generalizes perfectly to rates 50 and 200 without modification.
key_points: CONFIRMED (iter-2 h-main): Recall improved from 82.9% (29/35) to 100% (35/35), exceeding the ≥90% target. Precision held at 100%. The fix was adding an adaptive phase that detects cache-degraded configs and cross-explores scheduler × max-concurrency combinations (SJF × {64, 128}) rather than testing these knobs independently.

CONFIRMED (iter-2 h-robustness): The same 200-eval algorithm achieves 100% recall at rate=50 (23/23 tuples) and rate=200 (41/41 tuples), far exceeding the ≥80% threshold. The Pareto front grows with load (23→35→41 unique tradeoff tuples), and the adaptive degradation detection adjusts automatically to rate-dependent thresholds.

KEY INSIGHT: The missed Pareto points in iter-1 were caused by a scheduler×concurrency interaction that only appears under cache pressure — SJF+maxr=128 yields ~7% higher throughput than FCFS+maxr=256 in degraded regimes, at the cost of higher tail latency (e.g., 29.26 vs 28.64 rps but 1812 vs 1585ms ttft_p99). Independent knob exploration completely misses this.

STILL UNKNOWN: Whether the algorithm generalizes to other model architectures/sizes beyond qwen/qwen3-14b, and whether ≥90% recall is achievable with half the budget (100 evaluations). The 95% ceiling threshold for degradation detection has not been stress-tested across different workload characteristics (prefix token counts, request distributions).

RECOMMENDED NEXT (iter-3): Test model generalization (e.g., a different architecture or size class) and/or budget compression (target ≥90% recall at budget=100) to establish whether the approach is broadly applicable and cost-efficient.
